speechtext:

Speaker, I rise to move a motion under the provisions of Standing Order 43. In 1919, and again in 1972, Canadian veterans were led to believe that their government would tie their pensions to the average wage of five specific categories of unskilled workers in the public service. Since veterans pensions lag a full $900 behind that average wage adjustment despite adjustments in response to increases in the Consumer Price Index, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Munro):

speechtext:

subsubtopic: QUERY RESPECTING POSSIBLE IMPOSITION OF WAGE AND PRICE CONTROLS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in the absence of the Prime Minister my question is for the Acting Prime Minister, as the head of government. Is the government giving consideration now, or at all, to the imposition in any form of wage or price controls?

May 12, 1982
Oral Questions

subsubtopic: QUERY RESPECTING POSSIBLE IMPOSITION OF WAGE AND PRICE CONTROLS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I would ask the hon. member to read the comments made by the Minister of Finance before a standing committee of the House last week, if I remember correctly. In answer to a question from one of the members during consideration in committee, the Minister of Finance clearly and unequivocally indicated that he had no intention of imposing such controls.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would ask the Acting Prime Minister a second question. Is the government giving any consideration now, or at all, to pegging interest rates in this country in any way?
[ Translation]

Madam Speaker, the hon. member would do well to refer to the speech made by the Minister of Finance yesterday to his counterparts at the OECD in Paris. He would realize that the Minister of Finance, on that occasion, reiterated the Canadian government's intention of carrying on with its fight against inflation and invited his OECD counterparts to do the same, in order to provide for a steady and gradual recovery of the economy. In this context, he also said that if the nominal interest rates prevailing in the United States are compared with the real rates, there is a very substantial margin, which could be used by American financial authorities to relieve the pressure of current high interest rates on all industrialized countries.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: The Acting Prime Minister seems to be struck dumb. I will try once again.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Madam Speaker, is the government giving any consideration now, or at all, to the devaluation of the Canadian dollar?

Madam Speaker, it is clear from the hon. member's question that he reads the papers and has an ear for rumours.
However, speaking for the government, I can inform the hon. member straight away that the government has no intention, and that it has never been the intention of the Minister of Finance, to whom I was talking a few minutes ago, of devaluating the dollar.
The House will recall that at the First Ministers' Conference held last February, some of the provincial premiers had suggested this course of action. At the end of the conference
the Prime Minister made it clear that a decision to devaluate would have a disastrous effect, and the government's policy has not changed in this respect.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I have one last brief supplementary question for the dumb Acting Prime Minister. Is the government giving any consideration now, or at all, to the imposition of foreign exchange controls in any form?
Madam Speaker, I think I should answer that question.
Hear, hear!

The reason I did not answer the previous questions is that the Minister of State for Finance is obviously much more informed about the thinking of the Minister of Finance and follows these matters much more closely than I. For example, I spent a good part of the morning with the Premier of Nova Scotia, which the Minister of State for Finance was not required to do.
However, to answer the question, I would like to state, as the Minister of State for Finance did, that nothing the Minister of Finance has said can be taken to mean that there is any shift in the government's anti-inflationary policy.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: What about foreign exchange controls?

Furthermore, our policy with respect to the Canadian dollar remains the same. No devaluation of the dollar is being contemplated. I am obviously reading from a document which I received from the Minister of Finance. He has confirmed this to us today from Helsinki where, 1 am sure everyone knows, he is attending the International Monetary Fund meeting.

subtopic: QUERY RESPECTING GOVERNMENT POLICIES ON INFLATION AND UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the hon. member should look up the basic principles of economics. He ought to know that as soon as we are able to eliminate the climate of uncertainty in our economy by reducing inflationary expectations and reducing inflation rates, the resulting economic climate will favour increased investment and economic recovery, not only on a short term but on a sustained basis. subtopic: OIL AND GAS DRILLING IN OFFSHORE AREAS-PUBLICATION OF MEMORANDUM OF UNDERSTANDING ON ENVIRONMENT
OIL AND GAS DRILLING IN OFFSHORE AREAS-PUBLICATION OF MEMORANDUM OF UNDERSTANDING ON ENVIRONMENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. Two years ago, I believe, as the minister knows, the Ixtoc well in the Gulf of Mexico blew over three million barrels of oil into environment. Despite the best technology in the world, it took seven months to cap it. On Monday, outside the House, the minister announced a five-year, $600 million gas and oil exploration program in the Mackenzie Delta and in the Beaufort Sea, two thirds of the costs of which will be carried
Oral Questions
by the Canadian taxpayers. The majority of that drilling will be in extremely sensitive offshore areas where it will, without question, disrupt wildlife and fisheries. According to the government's own sources, should there be a spill or blowout there is not the technology in Canada to deal with such a disaster.
Since the minister promised on June 18 to make public an environmental memorandum of understanding on the offshore, why has it never been made public?

speakeroldname: Hon. Marc Lalonde (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: OIL AND GAS DRILLING IN OFFSHORE AREAS-PUBLICATION OF MEMORANDUM OF UNDERSTANDING ON ENVIRONMENT
speechtext: Madam Speaker, would the hon. member specify the memorandum of understanding to which he is referring? If he is referring to a specific agreement which has been signed, I will certainly be very happy to make it available. I am sorry I do not have the exact reference.

subtopic: OIL AND GAS DRILLING IN OFFSHORE AREAS-PUBLICATION OF MEMORANDUM OF UNDERSTANDING ON ENVIRONMENT
speechtext: The memorandum of understanding is the understanding between EMR, DIAND, the Department of the Environment all the different departments which are responsible for monitoring the environment. Perhaps the minister could respond to that.

My supplementary question is directed to the minister. As the minister knows, the taxpayers will carry two thirds of the costs of this five-year drilling program, and the public has a right to know that thorough, scientifically sound steps are being taken to protect the environment. These steps are not being taken now, as the minister knows, and provisions of Bill C-48 are being mobilized for the oil industry to get the rigs out there and to get the drilling going, but concerning protection for the environment, the baseline studies and so on have not been done and are not being done. I wonder if the minister would explain why the advisory committees provided for in Bill C-48, of which he is very well aware, have not been set up.

speakeroldname: Hon. Marc Lalonde (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
I would be very happy to make available the documents to which the hon. member refers. 1 think they may take the form of an exchange of letters between the ministers, if what he was referring to was an understanding between the departments.
As far as the latter point is concerned, I want to draw to his attention that the Government of Canada has the highest standard in terms of environmental protection offshore and in the Arctic. The fact is that for several years there has been exploration in the Arctic and offshore in Canada, and there has not been a single incident in terms of environmental hazard or accident-not one. This is testimony to the quality of the environmental concerns, the inspection, and the high standards that have been set by the Government of Canada to protect that very fragile environment. It is a concern that this

May 12, 1982
Presence in Gallery
government has very much at heart. The companies are required to take a number of steps with regard to the environment.
In addition, as late as Monday of this week, the Government of Canada released a study by the environmental assessment review panel dealing with the Beaufort Sea situation. All the information we have is made public as soon as it becomes available. I can tell the hon. member that we have been exploring for over ten years and there has not been a single incident or accident. We have been able to ensure that the environment is protected. That is testimony to the quality of the work being done by the officials in the government in that regard.

subtopic: ACCESS TO FUNDS FOR ENVIRONMENTAL STUDIES
ACCESS TO FUNDS FOR ENVIRONMENTAL STUDIES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is nice to know that there are a lot of words in Bill C-48 and that all these things are being done, but the memorandum of understanding on environmental matters has not been made public. The minister promised that last June. No advisory committees have been set up to look into environmental matters in the Mackenzie Delta or the Beaufort. The minister sent me a letter last week, in which he said the following:
The environmental studies revolving fund is an integral part of the Canada Oil and Gas Act. Its purpose is to provide the regulatory agency, the Canada Oil Gas Lands Administration (COGLA), with the information base for its decisions regarding hydrocarbon exploration and development.
I see the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development is here now. However, perhaps the minister can tell us why it is the $15 million revolving fund for environmental studies is inaccessible to native groups, concerned scientists and the public. They cannot get at those moneys. Would he tell us today how groups can get hold of that money and where they go to get it, because those studies should be under way now, not two or three years after the drilling?
Hon. Marc Lalonde (Minister of Energy, Mines and
Resources): Madam Speaker, the hon. member made a number of statements in his question. I will take the time to answer only some of them. He says no advisory body has been set up. I just told him that on Monday of this week a report by the environmental assessment review panel on environmental protection in the Beaufort Sea area was made public. Therefore, there are things taking place. Documents are being made public. I suggest to my friend that he is wrong in some of the assertions he is making.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is for the minister responsible for housing. In a number of meetings with the various regional caucuses of this House they have made the case that the funding available under the Canada Rental Supply Plan, the $7,500 interest-free loan, is not being taken up by builders because it is not enough to close the gap between the economic rent for an apartment unit and the market rent. speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
subsubtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF CANADA RENTAL SUPPLY PLAN
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I thank the hon. member for the question. It gives me the opportunity of saying that 1 have, on two occasions this week, met with representatives of HUDAC and their executive.
I also take the opportunity to indicate to the hon. member that the Canada Rental Supply Plan which speaks of the $7,500 per unit grant is advertised as a target mark. In the program which has been distributed and made available to interested developers across the country, we have said to them that we will not turn these down, that in any application which requests a grant larger than $7,500 the developer will have to indicate what the cost factors are that require a grant for a higher amount. Madam Speaker, I would like to indicate as well at this time that since the program has been advertised, which was roughly three weeks ago, the corporation has received approximately 2,000 inquiries, and we are now in the process of dealing with individual applicants to see if some of those projects will get started.

speakeroldname: Hon. James A. McGrath (St. John's East):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the minister keeps referring to this as a grant, which I think is part of the problem, because it is not a grant. He knows full well it is a loan that has to be amortized by the builder and consequently adds to his cost of financing.
I would like to change the subject, Madam Speaker, and ask the minister what the government intends to do with respect to the disastrous situation prevailing in the housing industry with regard to single family units. The minister knows that the
May 12, 1982

seasonably adjusted rate right now is 146,000, and that appears to be seriously inflated. The projections for the year, by all the forecasts, including CMHC, show there is going to be a disastrous situation of only 135,000 starts. There is going to be a shortfall, taking into account the shortfall for the last three years, of 211,000 units. That will drive up the cost of housing even more because it will reduce the supply of housing.
The minister knows that housing is the most labour-intensive industry in the country. I would ask the minister what recommendation he has for the government or for the House, what advice he has for the building industry in Canada, which is on the verge of collapse unless the minister is prepared to act.

Gotlieb, Under Secretary of State for External Affairs, stating in part: "However, review of the policy indicates that it would be appropriate within its expressed parameters for the ambassadors to Paris and Washington and High Commissioner to London to use first class air transportation on official business within the limitations set in the Treasury Board directive ..." and, if so, how does the government justify this statement with the directive on air travel issued by the Treasury Board dated September, 1980?

Did Mr. Pitfield authorize first class travel to Paris, Washington and London for those of ambassadorial class but not to Bonn and Tokyo and, if so (a) for what reason (b) was Mr. Pitfield enunciating a government policy that (i) Bonn and Tokyo are not as important as Paris, Washington and London (ii) the ambassadors to Bonn and Tokyo are not as important as Canada's representatives in Paris, Washington and London?

subsubtopic: DIRECTIVE ON TRAVEL
speechtext:
1. Yes.
2.	Yes. Section 3.2.3. of chapter 370 of the Administrative Policy Manual, based on a December, 1975, Treasury Board decision, relates to the comfort of employees on travel status and considerations of cost. The authority, issued in January, 1981, to utilize first class travel contained in Treasury Board Circular No. 1981-8 (T.B. 775270) is based on the recognition that the inherent workload of certain senior public service positions is such that incumbents might reasonably be expected to have to work while on travel status. The facilities in first class, both on the ground and in the air, are clearly more conducive to effective work resulting in cost effective travel time and have been authorized on that basis.

He said: Madam Speaker, the members of this House are probably wondering why, since we have already had an opportunity to consider a borrowing authority bill at second reading, we are coming back today with another borrowing authority bill for second reading.
Mr. Speaker, we are resuming second reading of the borrowing authority bill because during the debate on the previous bill, some hon. members expressed their concern that the bill contained three parts, namely, borrowing authority for the government, a number of amendments to the Excise Tax Act and the third part, a number of revenue tax measures relating to petroleum and natural gas.
As usual, the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Pinard) gave careful consideration to the representations made by hon.
May 12, 1982

members. There were meetings of the various party critics and myself and also meetings of the government, official opposition and New Democratic House leaders, and we finally agreed to split Bill C-93, so that the House could consider a separate bill on borrowing authority and another bill that would relate to the taxation aspect, namely, the amendments to the Excise Tax Act and the series of amendments regarding petroleum and natural gas revenue taxes. These negotiations also resulted in an agreement on the period of time the House would allocate to consideration of the respective bills, at all stages, including, second reading, with consideration in the standing committee as far as borrowing authority is concerned, and consideration in Committee of the Whole of the bill providing for amendments to the Excise Tax Act and petroleum and natural gas revenue taxes, and finally, approval in the House of these bills. Mr. Speaker, I would like to recall briefly what I said on second reading of Bill C-93. The purpose of this bill is to provide for supplementary borrowing authority for the government to cover the financial year 1982-83.
The highlights of Bill C-93 now Bill C- 111 which we are considering today, have already been discussed. It is perhaps useful to recall that the bill is seeking borrowing authority for $6.6 billion, and that all unused borrowing authority granted under the Borrowing Authority Act, 1981-82, and in excess of $3 billion has expired. This means that the balance of less than $3 billion will be carried over to the new fiscal year. The new borrowing authority of $6.6 billion being sought corresponds to budgetary and non-budgetary requirements for 1982-83 as set forth in the budget brought down in the House last November by the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen).
In addition to covering requirements set forth in the budget speech, as is customary, we shall require some room to mano-euver in order to deal with any contingencies that may arise as a result of exchange transactions or other eventualities. In past years, this contingency fund has remained at about $3 billion and has usually been added to the total borrowing requirements presented by the government. This year, however, the $3 billion or what will be left of the 1981-82 borrowing authority if the balance is less than $3 billion, as I said earlier, will not automatically lapse at the end of the financial year, and thus this remainder which is less than $3 billion can then be carried over. Consequently, that amount will be the government's contingency fund for 1982-83. The provision referring to the government's authority to contract and reimburse loans in foreign currency is a technical one, and the House will recall that this provision was also included, and I said earlier, in previous borrowing authority bills, and more specifically in the last four.
I would like to give an overview of the government's borrowing transactions since the beginning of the current financial year, and of the amount of borrowing authority used. As for the Borrowing Authority Act for 1981-82, which provided a
Borrowing Authority Act
new borrowing authority of $14 billion, the House will recall that this legislation received royal assent on April 8, 1981. Consequently, the debt program covered by this borrowing authority started at that time. From April 8, 1981 to March 31, 1982, the government borrowed a total of $9.9 billion in new funds on domestic markets. Of that amount, $9.3 billion was obtained through Canada Savings Bonds, $3.1 billion through marketable bonds, while net Treasury bill redemptions reduced the amount borrowed by $2.5 billion. As far as the marketable bond program is concerned, $0.1 billion is tied to foreign markets. These markets have provided the government with $300 million, thanks to the private sale of an issue to the central banks of Saudi Arabia. There was also a partial repayment on a loan of $700 million, which was due on March 8, 1982. Considering the spirit of co-operation existing on all sides with a view to limiting the debate on this new bill, I would rather not impose any further on the time of the House, and I would give other members an opportunity to take part in this debate. However, I would just like to refer to some of the points made in the previous debate on Bill C-93 and comment briefly, while further details could be given when the bill is considered in Committee of the Whole.
During the previous debate, one hon. member remarked that the petroleum revenue tax was supposed to increase federal revenues by several billion dollars. If I remember correctly, two different figures appeared in the English and French versions of Hansard. I would like to give the exact figure for federal revenues collected in the form of petroleum and gas revenue taxes and tax on additional oil revenues, namely, $23.2 billion for the period from 1981-82 to 1985-86. I am giving this figure to remove any misunderstanding that might have been caused by the fact that two different figures were printed in the respective versions of Hansard.
One of the points raised concerned the figure quoted in the estimates for the percentage of increase in government expenditures. I may inform the member for Etobicoke Centre (Mr. Wilson) that his explanation was not quite accurate. Expenditures in 1981-82 increased by 16.3 per cent, and not 22.3 per cent, as the hon. member stated. In 1980-81, petroleum compensation payments exceeded revenues by $2.7 billion. In 1981-82, payments more or less balanced revenues, which explains why there is no negative balance here. It is always possible to juggle figures and delete an item that is decreasing in order to get an expenditure total to increase more rapidly. It is also possible to delete an item that is increasing faster than total expenditures, for instance, debt servicing, in order to slow down the rate of increase of the total amount. But this is mere juggling with figures and actually does not prove anything. In any case, the real increase in total expenditures is, officially, 16.3 per cent.
During the previous debate, it was observed that expenditure increases should be brought back to the rate mentioned by the Minister of Finance in his budget speech, namely, they should

May 12, 1982
Borrowing Authority Act
be kept at a level below the growth rate of the national economy. I may point out that the government is maintaining its objective to keep the growth rate of its expenditures below that of our economy. This is reflected in the lower ratio of budgetary expenditures to gross national product, which dropped from 21.2 per cent in 1975-76 to 20 per cent in 1980-81. During that period, government expenditure objectives were set according to a broader concept, namely, that of total expenditures, in other words, the sum of budgetary expenditures and capital loans and non-budgetary advances. So, from 1976 to 1980, total expenditures increased at a slower rate than the nominal gross national product. During that period, the gross national product increased, respectively, by 9.3 per cent, 10.3 per cent, 13.7 per cent and 10.7 per cent, while total expenditures increased by 6.6 per cent, 9.3 per cent, 7.9 per cent and 8.8 per cent. During the debate, there were also some comments on the government's justification for its borrowing authority request. Mr. Speaker, I should like very briefly to remind the House of the government's commitment to take a far more rigorous approach to the management of public funds and thus bring about a reduction in the deficit. These objectives involve a policy of restraint that should help relieve inflationary pressures and promote the development of a better climate for economic recovery in our country.
As a result of the debt program, $9.9 billion of the borrowing authority of $14 billion approved for 1981-82 was used, as I said earlier, while $1.1 billion lapsed on March 31, 1982, and $3 billion was carried over to 1982-83, to be used for contingencies, as I explained a moment ago. Mr. Speaker, I should like to comment on further questions raised by hon. members. It was asked, for instance, why the government needed new borrowing authority for $6.6 billion at this time, when, and I believe it was the hon. member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) who made this comment, when the government's cash balance is high and it has already received $12 billion for 1980-81 and $14 billion for 1981-82.
In answer to the last part of the question, I would like to point out that the entire unused borrowing authority for 198081 lapsed on March 31, 1981, and the entire unused borrowing authority for 1981-82, in excess of the $3 billion to which I am constantly referring, also lapsed on March 31, 1982, and consequently, the only borrowing authority available to the government for 1982-83 is this sum of $3 billion which has not expired and which represents the government's contingency fund for 1982-83. Mr. Speaker, I would now like to answer that part of the question dealing with cash balances which at the beginning of the new financial year amounted to $6.6 billion. At the end of the financial year, a reasonably high level of deposits is necessary in order to cope with strong seasonal demand during the first quarter of each new financial year.
In addition, the government cannot let its deposits drop to zero, that is quite obvious. We have deposits for our daily transactions and also for contingencies, for instance, to respond to demand created by foreign exchange markets. In addition, let us not forget that deposits give the government some room for manoeuvring in managing its debt program, a fact that is particularly important in periods where interest rates are very volatile. I may add that the deposit amount in excess of $100 million produces 90 per cent of the interest of 91-day Treasury bills.
Mr. Speaker, several hon. members also criticized the government with respect to the 19.5 per cent interest paid on Canada Savings Bonds. One hon. member alleged that the government was paying 19.5 per cent on Canada Savings Bonds at a time when all indicators showed that rates were declining and that sales of Canada Savings Bonds would add $1 billion to the national debt and to the burden of Canadian taxpayers. Mr. Speaker, here I would like to point out that the government cannot plan its debt program according to the forecast for interest rate trends, and that it must take into account the situation existing at the time the bonds are put on the market to compete with other savings instruments. The cost of the 1981-82 issue of Canada Savings Bonds was much closer than usual to competitive interest rates. Over one million people purchased Canada Savings Bonds and it takes at least five weeks before paycheck deductions can begin. All these sales take some time.
During the campaign, interest rates fluctuated, and this made the yield of Canada Savings Bonds very attractive, since all interest rates on the market on other savings instruments were on a downward trend. With hindsight, it is easy to claim, this volatility having taken its toll, that the rate on Canada Savings Bonds was too high. However, this was not obvious when the rate was set for the marketing of Canada Savings Bonds. It is important for the government to set an equitable rate as well as a competitive rate for this instrument, which must compete with other savings instruments on the market. The sales of Canada Savings Bonds will not add one billion dollars to the cost of the debt since the product of the sales was used to pay the negotiable debt which was falling due and would have had to be renewed otherwise. Until November 1981, for the previous 18 months, Canada Savings Bonds were, all in all, the least costly source of funds for the government.
As a final point, I would like to refer to another aspect of debt management which was raised during the debate on Bill C-93. Based on the different percentages of the various borrowing instruments of the government, some members wondered whether the government had changed its policy of using short-term instruments rather than medium or long-term instruments to finance its debt. I believe, Mr. Speaker, that the diversity of the borrowing instruments available to the government to manage its debt can be explained by the fact that this allows the government to use some flexibility in adjusting to
May 12, 1982

existing conditions on the market when it needs to borrow. That is the reason why there have been a number of variations over these last few months, for instance, a larger rate of financing through Canada Savings Bonds. This signals no basic change in the government policy of debt management. Simply, the government used the tools at its disposal and the flexibility needed to adapt to the extremely volatile conditions it was facing on the marketplace.
Mr. Speaker, I indicated at the beginning of my remarks that under the agreement reached by all parties in this House on this legislation and the one that is to follow tomorrow, there is a time limitation. Therefore, I will not take too much of the time of the House, but I simply wanted to give a few explanations following some remarks that were made in the preceding debate, and 1 am sure we will have an opportunity for a very fruitful debate at the committee stage, to further the consideration of this legislation. I would like to thank the House leaders of the government, of the Official Opposition and of the New Democratic Party as well as the party spokesmen since we have agreed to a much more expeditious consideration of these two bills.

Mr. Speaker, I will speak very briefly on this bill at this stage because I spoke at length on second reading. I want to point out to the House and to the country in general that Bill C-93 was opposed by this party on the same basis as Bill C-94, on which bells rang on an adjournment motion for over 15 or 16 days. If the government had any sense, it would never have introduced Bill C-93 in the way in which it was introduced. 1 compliment the government on finally coming to reason. This bill is a bad bill and so are the tax provisions contained in the balance of Bill C-93, which will be debated under Bill C-112 tomorrow. However, if it were not for this party putting extreme pressure on the government, this bill would not have been divided. We would not be debating Bill C- 111 today. 1 say to Your Honour and to the country that we are at last seeing some democracy around here. At least the people have an opportunity for input. At least we are reaching a situation where, under the terms of reference of this bill, even though debate will be somewhat limited, the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) will be required to come before the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs to explain the financial policies of the government. Your Honour knows that the minister always tries to avoid coming before the standing committee, so for the first time, we will be able to have the minister before us again for two full sessions to explain why he needs to borrow $6.6 billion.
The question of $6.6 billion came out of the air. It was a figure in the budget. But we all know, and the country knows, that the budget of the Minister of Finance is just so much air, smoke and feathers. It is really not a budget at all. It has no particular approaches in it which make sense. The country cannot go along with it. The minister made at least changes to
Borrowing Authority Act
it, and there are still more changes coming up. So we expect the minister, either in the House or before the committee, to explain to us and to the country in general a new financial policy which must be proposed by this government.
Speaking to the question of the Canada Savings Bonds issue, it clearly costs the country at least $1 billion. It was clear to any intelligent person in the financial market, in August, that 19.5 per cent was too much money to pay for interest. It became clearer in September and even more clear in October. It became an absolute certainty in November, yet the bond sale was held open until November 6. If there was ever a government incompetent at borrowing money, it is this government, and for that reason alone this bill must be opposed.

Mr. Speaker, there was a time, not too long ago, maybe as recently as the last year or so, when I looked forward to getting on a plane, travelling back to my constituency, meeting with my people and trying to hear and solve their problems. I must say that as I think about that prospect for this week and next week, I do not feel good about it because I know that when I walk down the street or go to my office, I will meet a group of young people who will be looking for jobs which I cannot help them to find.
The community in which I live was once a progressive, growing community of Fraser Valley West. At one time, if the people of Langley and Surrey who came to my office really wanted a job, I could find places for them. I could send them here or there. But now, all of a sudden, for the first time in some time I send them on the circuit, and they come back empty-handed. Instead of simply finding no jobs, they are unfortunately finding, again and again, that businesses have gone bankrupt. So it is not only those seeking jobs in the business community who are suffering, but it is also the business community which is suffering to a very great extent these days. This hurts. It hurts when I see these massive cutoffs. I see professional people and small business people who have always had jobs in the last 15 or 20 years but now, not only have their jobs run out, but their unemployment insurance has run out as well. As the unemployment insurance runs out, they fall on to the welfare system, which makes them lose their confidence and self-respect. We see a new kind of depression, which is indeed disgusting and discouraging in this great country.
It is not that the potential is any less this year than it was last year, or five years ago; rather, it is that something has gone wrong with the direction of our economy. That direction has been consistently pursued by the Liberal government which has its mind set or a set attitude toward possible solutions. We find that every time the government comes forward with a solution, it is an obsession. It is obsessed with overtaxing, over-borrowing or government intervention. It constantly seems to want the people to give to the government so that the government may redistribute and thus somehow solve the problem. If the government does not have sufficient money

May 12, 1982
Borrowing Authority Act
from taxes, it then goes out and borrows it, regardless of the cost. The government has the attitude that it somehow has the answer.
Our society has followed a long trend, one in which we had a great deal of confidence in professionals and in an elitist, intellectual policy. We have stopped looking to ourselve and have started looking toward others. We have cast responsibility on to governments. Of course, the government assumes the responsibility, and to pay for it, collects taxes. The government taxes to a certain point, and when it can tax no more, it begins to borrow, and here we are.
It is pretty hard for me to tell the unemployed persons from Langley or Surrey that we will go out and borrow billions more dollars on their behalf and that somehow we will get the economy going through government intervention, government bureaucracy, government regulations, and that the government will create jobs. That confidence, that mind-set, must change.
I am not saying to the minister who just spoke that the government which sits opposite is morally wrong or that it is trying to do the wrong thing morally. It is not trying to drive the country into bankruptcy. It is not trying to drive the people along. Maybe it is trying to drive the people to unemployment to cure inflation, because that is the solution it sees: more unemployment to cure inflation. But, instead, we get more unemployment and more inflation. The solutions are not working. Although the idea is right, the solution to implement the idea is wrong. Morally, we all want the same thing, a stronger, better Canada, full of opportunity for all our citizens, but we need to change the idea of solutions. The solutions lie in ridding the economy of unwarranted and unneeded regulations, simply the factor of regulation, the restriction of regulations, the requirements.
I wonder how many members opposite, instead of simply buying a house, have gone through the process of trying to build a house, the process of regulation, the process of requirement. Last week I attended the Surrey Volunteers dinner, and Ivy Adamson, an old pioneer of Surrey, the first alder-woman in Surrey, said, "When I first came on council here, there were a bunch of tarpaper shacks. People started with little shacks and they started building houses for themselves. What a shame it is that in today's society we cannot start to build again modestly, what a shame that this opportunity has been taken away from us, because we now require a $150,000 house instead of providing for our basic needs." It is overregulation and overrequirement.
We must also try to develop a freer trade policy. We keep thinking and teaching others as though we were an island unto ourselves and as though somehow Canada, by putting up higher and higher tariffs, will create more and more jobs here.
I think history shows that creating more and more tariffs might create a job for a day or even a decade. All too often those tariffs turn into subsidies. In fact, they become counterproductive to the point that the whole economic system begins to break down and we lose our capacity to compete in international markets. We must have policies and solutions that work toward freer trade. The only way to create a stronger economic
lifestyle is to sell what we produce. Everything we now produce in Canada we can use. This is a small market, so it does not do any good just to produce those things that wear out and need to be replaced. That is not good enough. We have to look to the great markets of the world. If we place tariff upon tariff upon tariff and exclude trade from other markets, they will excude us from their markets. There will be no jobs in Ontario, British Columbia or anywhere else in Canada. Free trade relations in the world need to be expanded by reducing tariff barriers, thus working toward freer trade.
We need to cut government spending. We are not doing that with this provision. What we are doing is borrowing more money. How many people want the government to borrow more? Do they want their government to spend $6 billion today? At 20 per cent interest, who is going to pay? It will be our children. They will pay and pay the deficit created by this bill.
That is not what Canadians want. They want government spending cut back. They want less government not more government and more regulation. Canadians want that, as was demonstrated in Saskatchewan.
Does this bill give us more? No, it gives us less and less because we are getting more and more government. There is less and less responsibility for the individual and more and more for the government. You cannot cut government spending by borrowing more. The more the government spends, the more we need to borrow on their behalf; the more taxes we pay, the more they spend.
Let us talk about government cutting spending, not expanding it. However, that is what is being done today, creating more government and more tax burden, and we will have to pay for this at 19 or 20 per cent.
In addition to cutting spending, we must restore incentives. I talked with workers in the housing industry. I asked them why they did not stay an extra couple of hours to complete a job rather than putting all their tools away and having to come back the next morning. They replied that they would get overtime, but the government would just take it away in taxes. How many times do we hear people ask, "Why work longer, why produce more?" There is no incentive left in our society.
It is time to rebuild the incentive society. It is the motive of profit and the individual getting ahead that created the wealth of this nation and of the rest of this world. It worked before, so why not give it a chance to work again?
We must cut government spending and cut taxes. Everyone says that is a dream; whoever heard of a government cutting taxes, it just does not happen. It does happen and it is happening. It is happening right here on our continent. Not only is it happening, but it is working again. This is not the first time.
Our biggest problem is inflation. We will not solve that problem by borrowing more or by increasing interest rates, which is what we are doing today. Instead, we should be
May 12, 1982

working for a tax cut. That is what President Reagan did in the United States. He implemented a 30 per cent across-the-board tax cut. It was not just for the big guys, but also for the little guys, the middle guys and everyone in between.
Is there a Canadian today who does not want a tax cut? Some may say it would not be good, but maybe at this time it would be. What did the tax cut and control of government spending do in the United States? It cut the inflation rate to zero.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I know the finance critic for the Progressive Conservative Party indicated he would advocate that the policies of Ronald Reagan be applied in Canada. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if the hon. member will listen to my speech, I will tell him about supply-side economics. That is the basic text of my speech today. I support those points and I will tell him why. I support them, Mr. Socialist, because they work, and I will give an example of how they work.
The brother of the late President Kennedy is now promoting the same policies as our Liberal government. Let us see what President Kennedy did. In 1961 when John F. Kennedy took office, the unemployment rate stood at 6% per cent and the budget was in deficit by almost $4 billion. Between 1961 and 1966 real output as measured by constant dollar GNP grew at a 516 per cent annual rate. It grew. Our growth rate is going in the other direction. It is going down.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext: What is happening to the American growth rate?

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
It is going up, my friend, you just wait. The unemployment rate fell to less than 4 per cent and the federal
Borrowing Authority Act
budget moved to a roughly balanced position. That is what happened when President Kennedy applied a 30 per cent tax cut across the board. Inflation throughout the era averaged between 1 and 2 per cent annually, not 1 and 2 per cent a month as it is in Canada.
Surprising as it may seem, given the mythology surrounding Jack Kennedy, government spending as it relates to total output actually declined during the Kennedy era. Government spending declined. Some may say that is not the right medicine today, that it was the right medicine a decade and a half ago. President Reagan has begun to apply it, and it would be more effective if he did not have the brakes on him. It is working. Would anyone deny that it is working in the United States? Then, by a spillover-unfortunately by a spillover, not because of anything members opposite are going to do over there-we may benefit somewhat. But they should be prepared now for the recovery, not dragging deeper and deeper into recession and depression, and that depression is as bad as the recession.
The depression that I feel about the economy, the fear that I have to invest, the fear that I have to go out and create something new, that fear is real in my constituency. It is real amongst my people. We need a reinstall a new, strong attitude amongst those people. We have to recognize it. I hope it is the bottom. We might have to wait until 1985 for the turnaround in Canada, as they are experiencing it in the United States this year. We might have to wait a little longer. We might have to wait until we get rid of this government, because we cannot change their attitude. This borrowing bill is a perfect example. I hope the Canadian people will see it. Do you understand? Do you understand what 1 am saying? I hope so. Well, if you do not come and see me afterwards and we will talk about it.
We will get into the subject of supply now. Let us consider a little what these tax cuts are. In our society there is something called a resistance theory, not an astounding theory but a very interesting one. It was evolved by Professor Arthur Laffer. The professor made a statement saying that you can tax people and then you can tax them more and the government gets more money; you can tax people still more, and you get more money; you can tax more and more and more, until people get to the point where they say: "Just a minute, I am not paying any more tax, that is too much, I am not working any more because I am only working for the government, the government is taking more of my money than I get myself." We then find this resistance to taxation. So the more you tax, actually at that point the curve goes the other way and you start getting less revenue. This has proven to be true, the more you tax at a certain point, the less revenue you get. In order to get more revenue at that point you have to cut taxes. The main game in Canada right now amongst businessmen-it is survival, at the moment-generally, amongst those who are surviving, is to figure out how to get more disposable income, how to beat

May 12, 1982
Borrowing Authority Act
income tax, how to establish income tax shelters. The avoidance of income tax is the biggest game in town. Why? Because we have reached that peak where taxation becomes regressive, and to get more tax revenue we have in fact to cut taxes. That is what John F. Kennedy found in 1961 when he started his program. He cut the taxes by 30 per cent, and in the end he got more tax revenue. He got more tax revenue because by cutting taxes 30 per cent more people went to work. As more people went to work less people were being paid unemployment and welfare. Those people soon began paying unemployment insurance. They were producing some real goods that could be exchanged domestically and internationally. They could exchange those goods for real hard currency, for real money. In so doing the United States stabilized the dollar. The American dollar became so stabilized that they could in fact afford to go off the gold standard.
Unfortunately, through these heavy liberalized programs that we have experienced in the past 15 years, we have moved in the other direction, and the American dollar now is less stabilized. Perhaps the Americans need to do something as President Reagan said, to make the American dollar as good as gold. A lot of people are saying the U.S. is going in that direction. It may be that they will bring the gold standard back again, and make the American dollar good in that way. It is an interesting idea. If that happens, Canada must be ready. We may have to reconsider pegging our dollar.
What is happening to our dollar today while we are sitting here? It is dropping, and dropping very fast. It is at 80 cents, or 80.1. It is falling fast. I heard on the radio that it may drop to 77 cents. Some analysts are saying it will drop to 77 cents. It may be that we should think about pegging our dollar and making it good, too. It may be that we need to peg it at about 70 cents, but perhaps we should peg it at 75, 76, 77, 78, or 80 cents. I do not know what you are going to peg it at, but perhaps you had better peg it at some point and guarantee it. Let the Canadian government guarantee that dollar because if it guarantees that dollar, we can start controlling the interest rate a little better and we would not have our interest rates fluctuating up and down and being influenced so much by international markets. To stabilize that dollar, we would have to put some money again today into the money markets. If it were pegged, it could be stabilized and that stabilization of the dollar would mean we could then work on the interest rates. That is what we have to do now.
I would be happy if the Liberal government would wake up to supply side economics, if they would swallow their pride and look at the way it works. Then we could control inflation rates better, interest rates would begin to drop, and the unemployment rate would follow suit as sure as can be. That will drop as well. Why not take those good ideas and apply them? Some people say that that is fine for the Americans but that ours is a different stituation. That is a large model, they say, there are 250 million people there, that situation does not apply here.
Very well, let us take the other side and see if it has worked anywhere else. Let us go to a smaller model, let us go to Puerto Rico and see what has happened there. Under Governor Romero's leadership, income tax in Puerto Rico has been

I've been involved in forestry for 35 years and the job situation now is the worst since about 1947. There's been ups and downs but never as bad as this year. Maybe 25 per cent of the student body will find jobs ... normally it's 90 per cent at the time of graduation.
Other technical students, including mining students, are experiencing setbacks.
The branch manager of BCIT's Canada Employment Centre said:
Right now, the opportunities are dismal. Usually 90 to 95 per cent find work but it will go a way down this year. They could get work fighting fires-
Even that is no longer present. He went on to say:
-students cannot look to the public service sector for help.
BCIT noted as well that the number of employers recruiting on its campus is significantly less this year. I also point out that the situation at Simon Fraser University for graduates of that university is very much the same. The summer job market is bleak. It is the bleakest it has been for post-secondary students in many, many years. The housing situation facing post-secondary education students is impossible. A young man came to my constituency office a month ago. He told me that he worked for two years to save enough money to study at technical school. What kind of waste of human resources in the country is that? What kind of waste is that which is being duplicated across the land?
It is young people who are being particularly adversely affected by the economic policies of government and it is also women. I should like to point out the serious impact of government economic policies on women and the failure of this particular piece of legislation to come to terms with that devastating impact. We know that traditionally the unemployment rate for women is higher than it is for men and that in times of economic crises, such as those we face now, this problem is exacerbated by the last-hired-first-fired syndrome. Although the number of women entering the labour force has increased very significantly during the last ten years, basically more women are doing the same kind of work. Sixty per cent of all working women do three kinds of jobs-clerical jobs, sales jobs and service jobs. These are low-paying, dead-end jobs; in effect, they are job ghettos. In many of these areas we
are seeing significant lay-offs which disproportionately affect women and disproportionately affect young women.
Also we know that the wage gap between the wages of women and the wages of men is 60 per cent. For every dollar a man earns, a woman earns 60 cents. For example, in Canada in 1979 the average working woman earned $11,741 compared with the average man's salary of $18,537. Women do not only suffer from this wage gap at the present time, but as well when it comes time for a pension, including the Quebec pension plan and the Canada Pension Plan, their low pay follows them. Low pay means little or no pension benefits on retirement.
Basically the federal government has been providing lip service to remove this disparity. It acknowledges that the problem exists but it refuses to implement effective affirmative action programs to mitigate against this job ghetto and wage gap disparity. It insists upon voluntary affirmative action programs in the private sector, and the result of those has been a dismal failure. The last count shows that some 27 of 750 companies approached have signed such an agreement. Also we know that in this time of economic crisis there have been serious cutbacks in child care facilities which once again discriminate heavily against women. There is still a very small percentage of women in the management category. 1 believe there is some 4.3 per cent in the public service. The government's record on its commitment to equal pay for work of equal value is absolutely vacuous.
We know that there is nothing whatsoever in this budget and the bill which was introduced by the minister to assist the elderly and old age pensioners who are falling further and further behind. In 1980 some three million Canadians lived in poverty. Ten per cent of all Canadian families and 30 per cent of all single people were poor, according to statistics provided by the National Council of Welfare.
Perhaps the most searing indictment of this government's economic policies is the fact that over half of the single persons in Canada over the age of 70 live in poverty. Over two-thirds of the elderly women in Canada live in poverty. In this day and age, that statistic is an absolute disgrace.
There has been virtually no change in the distribution of income from 1951 to 1981. The bottom 20 per cent of families still receive 5.9 per cent and the top 20 per cent still get about 40 per cent, which is almost ten times as much. That figure has not changed over the last 30 years.

Our first proposal is for a massive injection of funds into the economy in order to create jobs in Canada. We must recognize that at this time in our history there is much work which needs to be done. Jobs could be created if only this government would take the initiative and put Canadians back to work instead of having them collect unemployment insurance and welfare.
We also believe that we must take control of the manufacturing sector in Canada which is now so heavily dominated by

foreign interests in general and American multinational corporations in particular. The government should revitalize our manufacturing sector and ensure a far greater proportion of research and development is carried out in Canada. We must immediately lower interest rates to break their stranglehold, particulary on small businesses on this country. We must eliminate the insidious situation where the only ones who profit from the economic policies of this government are the banks.

The most important step to take is to break the corporate stranglehold on our economy once and for all. This stranglehold on our economy is a result of the dominating pursuit of profit and greed. The pursuit of that profit and greed has led to the poverty we have seen, particularly among the elderly and single parents. Another result of this pursuit has been the destruction of our environment in many parts of Canada because the way to achieve greater profits is to cut corners. Profits will be greater if you do not take precautions to ensure that there is no pollution or that acid rain does not destroy the lakes of northern Ontario, that there is no arsenic poisoning in the Northwest Territories. The budget is divided roughly into four parts. Transfer payments account for 51 per cent of government expenditures, the public debt about 23 per cent, government operations about 16 per cent and national defence approximately 9.7 per cent.
If you go through the arguments of the opposition parties as we listen to them in the House or find them in newspapers or magazines, Mr. Speaker, you will find that while each party has a different emphasis on how it should spend money, or a different mix in the programs they project, the size of government and the totality of its budget would be really very little different from what we have today. In fact, I would argue that both would probably be larger then what we have today.
For example, in our transfer payments 51 cents of every dollar is transferred to provincial governments, corporations and individuals. I have not heard any spokesman for the two opposition parties suggest they would make any cuts, let alone sizeable cuts in any transfer payments to the three recipients I just mentioned. In fact, if you look at the rhetoric of the opposition parties, you will find that that portion of the budget would probably increase, and increase dramatically.

What about the public debt? It was not that long ago when the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark), on the verge of an electoral triumph in 1979, was talking about the need for a stimulative deficit, the need for the Government of Canada to go even deeper into debt in order to make those investments that would be necessary for a greater return, both privately and publicly, later in the decade. In light of that right hon. member's desire for a stimulative deficit, the demands by his colleagues for greater incentives to the business community and their strident demand that we give more to the provincial governments to help them look after education, medicare and social services of various sorts, I do not believe that party is committed to a reduction of the public debt.
If, Mr. Speaker, you have been following the arguments made in this House by members of the New Democratic Party, you will see that they are totally committed to a significant increase in the public debt. I am pleased to hear that at least they are honest enough to commit themselves so openly to increased indebtedness. They at least have the candour of their commitments, something which cannot be said about the party which forms the official opposition.
When we look at the cost of government operations, I doubt that the NDP would give us any reduction in this area. In fact, to deliver the types of programs they anticipate, there would be a significant increase in the size of government operations.
The official opposition party would probably make government operations slightly cheaper than they are right now. I do not know whether they would follow through with the slasher's desire to eliminate 60,000 public servants, but I expect we would see a determined attempt to reduce the size of government operations in the years ahead.
The trouble with cuts in government operations is that this is a minor cost of doing business, a minor cost in the government budget. No matter how rigorously you apply the paring knife to government operations, you will not find a lot of money. I suggest that the official opposition's desire and eagerness aside, any savings that would be found in a reduction of government operations would be minimal at best.
In the last category of budget expenditures, national defence, the New Democratic Party makes no attempt to hide its commitment to a lower defence budget. I believe I can say that without fear of contradiction. However, the official opposition has been equally candid in its projected policies in the area of national defence. When I go to my constituency, I rarely attend a meeting or a function without someone making the accusation that while the government is asking them to tighten their belts, the government itself is out of control and is spending money as though there were an unlimited supply.

First, there is the bureaucracy and the relationship between its executive management and labour. Second, there is the cabinet and its relationship with the bureaucracy. From what I can see, and 1 do not claim omniscience though some members opposite do, I would have to argue that no, this government is not out of control. Mr. Speaker, it was not that long ago that the Lambert Commission, the D'Avignon report and a succession of auditors general sounded the warning that this government was on the verge of being out of control. This government listened to those warnings and it acted on them so that we have today in place a very sophisticated and thorough management system which did not exist a few years ago.
I would like to take this opportunity to outline this management system so that all hon. members opposite, and the public with whom they talk, can understand that this government is making a very serious effort to discipline this very large and expensive government that has evolved over the last few decades.
First of all, Mr. Speaker, there is the fiscal plan. That is a five-year projection of the anticipated expenditures of the Government of Canada. Then inside each department, in an effort to create programs that can fit into that five-year plan, there are what are called departmental strategic overviews. These overviews represent an annual review of the objectives of each department, according to the planning guidelines generated by its parent cabinet committee. These reviews examine in detail the objectives of the department. They ask a number of important questions. Do the objectives of the department still make sense? If they make sense, to what extent has the department achieved those objectives, and at what cost? If it has not achieved those objectives, or if the cost is too high, are there reasonable alternatives?
Still within the department, Mr. Speaker, there are multiyear operational plans. These plans indicate the way in which each department attempts to realize the objectives enunciated in the strategic overview. The plans are continually updated and are submitted yearly to Treasury Board and the parent committee of cabinet, with accompanying additional evaluation plans, so that Treasury Board and cabinet have the information necessary to make a wise and prudent judgment of the performance of those departments.
Still within departments, Mr. Speaker, there is something called the budget year operational plan. This is an attempt by the department to establish the relationship between the estimates presented to Parliament and the department's management system.
Now moving on from the departments there is the very real accomplishment of the reform of the estimates. The reform of the estimates has its expression in three separate documents. The first document is the government expenditure plan which outlines the expenditure plans of the government in total and by envelope for a number of years in the future. The second document shows the appropriations necessary to carry out the plans outlined in the preceding document. Thirdly, still under development and not yet submitted, are the program evaluation plans which get down to the nitty-gritty of the expenditure of the dimes and the pennies necessary to carry out the appropriations which themselves flesh out the plans of the first document.
Supplementing all of these plans and estimates is the IMPAC program. This program is three years old. There are 25 plans that have evolved in 31 departments, covering 85 per cent of the expenditures of this government and covering 95 per cent of the government's employees.
Now, Mr. Speaker, if you take all the programs that I have just outlined in boring detail and look at their impact on the system and ask yourself, has the evolution of these programs, has the establishment of all of these planning systems and the recruiting of all of the staff necessary to carry out these evaluations and plans expeditiously and accurately all produced results? Have they managed to discipline the system that Lambert and others suggested was on the verge of uncontrollability?
If you look at the evidence, I think you would have to say that the results have proven the benefits and the wisdom of the system. The growth rate of the government in person-years has been curbed substantially. In 1975 there were 317,184 person-years in government. In 1981 there were 315,680 person-years; that is a decline, Mr. Speaker, an important decline.

roughly 16 per cent of the total budget. Mr. Speaker, 1 point out that it was not that long ago that the cost of government in Canada was 25 per cent of the budget. So while government is more expensive today, and I would not argue that it is not, as a proportion of the government's budget the cost of government is in fact coming down. I think that is another remarkable and laudable accomplishment of this government.
In the light of those accomplishments and in the light of the fact that the present Auditor General has nothing but muted criticisms and mild commendations to make of the government's performance, why do we not hear more about the successes of this government? Why do we-that is, the public-not have a greater understanding of this government's ability to discipline itself and to control its size and expenditures?
The answer is two-fold. First, good news, frankly, is no news. What does it profit an opposition to praise the government? No one on this side of the House should be waiting with bated breath for opposition members to say anything good about the very real and important steps this government has taken and about the resulting efficiency achieved over the last few years.
The second reason we do not hear much about the gains which have been made in government productivity or efficiency is the fact that, regrettably, most members of this House- certainly the vast bulk of members of the opposition-have never read the documents in which these plans and their successes have been documented. Quite frankly, most members of the opposition do not have the foggiest idea of how the system operates and because they do not have the foggiest idea, they are trapped in the outmoded rhetoric of the mid-1970s when most of their criticisms were beginning to emerge.
Finally, I would like to take this opportunity to assess the third and, as I said, perhaps the most serious criticism which has been made in this particular debate, and that is that this government has so mismanaged the economy that Canada is on the verge of collapse. Rutgers University appeared to document this perspective and to give it some intellectual legitimacy when it revealed in a report several weeks ago that of the executives in the seven industrialized nations it surveyed, the 4,200 Canadian executives were the most pessimistic. It was Canadians who, looking ahead to the future, concluded, unlike their counterparts in other countries, that there was nothing ahead except more doom and more gloom. I would argue that their predictions do not prove mismanagement of the economy. They offer nothing more than soft impressions and a psychological knee-jerk reaction to contemporary difficulties. They reflect the dark cloud syndrome in the Canadian psyche that opposition members-especially of the official opposition-so successfully manipulate in the debates in this House and on the hustings across Canada.

Its conclusion was that the Canadian economy had the second best record of performance in the industrialized world. When we realize that Japan was number one, second best in that study represents a remarkable achievement by the administrations which were in power during that period.
That is an American perspective, and to some hon. members opposite it may be tainted for that very reason. But there has been another report published more recently, this one in 1982 by the European Management Forum, which decided to research, evaluate and write a report on industrial competitiveness. The Forum evolved 241 criteria and applied them to 21 industrialized nations. As a result of its studies the Forum concluded that the Canadian economy was number five. It was not number 13, not number 20 or not number 21, as one might guess from the rhetoric of hon. members opposite; it was number five. I think that is a respectable placing. Japan was first, Switzerland second, the United States third and West Germany fourth.
As far as I am concerned, those two reports indicate conclusively that this government has had, if not the best record, certainly a fine record of achievement in the last two decades.
I am not ashamed of its performance. I am not prepared to apologize in this House to hon. members opposite for the performance of this government and for the performance of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau).
There is a sub-theme inside this theme of mismanagement, and that is that the Government of Canada interferes so badly in the Canadian economy and that the heavy hand of government is so pronounced-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-111 seeks to provide borrowing authority for $6.6 billion. That is a big item. It is a big ticket item, and the fact is that it is one

May 12, 1982
Borrowing Authority Act
in a series. This government will undoubtedly be back for more.
The hon. member who preceded me spoke about the fantastic record of this government over the last two decades. What is staggering is that 20 years ago this $6.6 billion figure represented the total federal government expenditures of Canada. Ten years ago it represented about one-half. Today the $6.6 billion represents roughly 10 per cent of total federal government expenditures. So we can see that the growth has been phenomenal and more Canadians are wondering where this trend will eventually lead us. Our expenditures and deficits are growing. We are spending more to service our debt. Our rate of growth is declining and production is stagnant. Canadians note that the only growth in Canada today is that of government, and that is not productive.
It is clear, Mr. Speaker, that this trend cannot continue. It is obvious that the direction of this country must change. I submit that we must reduce the level of government expenditures as a percentage of the GNP. Secondly, we must stimulate growth in production to generate new wealth. We must do this if we are to sustain the level of government services we have been accustomed to in this country, if we are to provide those less fortunate with the kind of support services we have in the past so they can live in dignity.
Let us briefly look at our current economic setting, Mr. Speaker. We all know our economy is in a shambles. This year, in spite of the Minister of Finance's (Mr. MacEachen) predictions of a $10.5 billion deficit, economists predict it will be in the order of $13 billion plus. Next year it is expected to rise to $14.5 billion as opposed to the budget forecast of $9.6 billion.
Why this trend towards higher deficits? There are a number of reasons. Number one, energy revenues are lower than originally anticipated; some suggest $20 billion or $30 billion less. Second, lower corporate incomes result in reduced income taxes collected. I note with interest, Mr. Speaker, that the CNR has reported the worst quarterly loss in its history, at $67 million for the first quarter of 1982. Compare that to its 1981 first quarter profit of $69.9 million. Other companies have experienced similar cutbacks in their profits. The oil companies are just one example. Banks have registered profit reductions in the order of 25 per cent to 30 per cent. It has been estimated that more than 50 per cent of the Vancouver business community will be applying for tax refunds this year. As of 1981 corporate profits are at their lowest level since 1947, when the national accounts were first published.
Third, there is the fact of escalating interest costs. We are now spending one dollar out of every five to service our debt. Last year there was an increase of 38 per cent in that category alone, and I suspect it will be higher this year.
Fourth, we continue to rely upon oil imports to supply domestic needs. This will not only have a negative effect on our balance of payments and budgetary transactions, but indeed it has a very significant effect on growth, development and job
creation in this country. It certainly has a major effect on the level of the Canadian dollar, which also impacts on interest rates.
Fifth, because of the slowdown and massive unemployment with more people being forced on unemployment insurance, welfare and other government social benefits, those costs will escalate, which will further increase government spending.
We are experiencing a stagnation in growth. It is now estimated that our growth is going to be minus one-half per cent in 1982, compared to a supposed increase of 2.2 per cent projected by the Minister of Finance.
I cite these points because it is clear that the Minister of Finance and his bureaucrats have clearly misread the behaviour of the economy. They have clearly been irresponsible in projecting the effects of the November 12 budget, and to me this kind of gross incompetence should trigger both the minister's and his advisers' resignation, if not that of the whole government. I say to you, Sir, that that would be the best way of improving business confidence in this country. But, of course, that is not about to happen.
The mess we are in is not something which materialized over the last year or so; rather it was over the last 14 years. It is part of a pattern. For example, since this Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) took office in 1968 we have only had one balanced budget, which was in 1969. If you look at his record further you will note that during the period 1968-82 we have accumulated budgetary deficits totalling approximately $90 billion. And the hon. member across the way asks, is this government out of control? You are darned right it is out of control, Mr. Speaker. Our national debt now stands at roughly $135 billion, or $14,260 per taxpayer, or $5,560 per capita.
