subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
I am not talking about Japan. This is the House of Commons of Canada, we are dealing with the Canadian economy, and that is what is important.
Interest on our national debt is some $16.6 billion a year. Put another way, it is $1,750 per taxpayer, or $680 per capita.
Looking at inflation, we know that in 1968 it was something in the order of 4 per cent. Today it is hovering around 12 per cent in spite of wage and price controls in 1975 which were supposed to see the rate of inflation drop to 4 per cent. In the day leading up to wage and price controls the Prime Minister said he had wrestled inflation to the ground. Well, it has been some match! The consumer price index has increased by 183 per cent, and the purchasing value of the dollar has fallen by some 70 per cent more or less since that man has taken office. In 1968 unemployment was 4.5 per cent; today it is about 9.6 per cent, or 1.2 million Canadians are unemployed. The bank rate was approximately 7.5 per cent in 1968; today it is around 16 per cent with customers having to pay anywhere from 18 per cent to 20 per cent. The Canadian dollar was worth 93 cents U.S. in 1968; today it is 81 cents and falling.
We have a shameful manufacturing deficit of $21 billion, the result of which has been 133,000 fewer manufacturing jobs
May 12, 1982

in 1982 compared in 1981. We have a current account deficit of $8 billion. Investment capital is flowing out of Canada at unprecedented levels, seven times greater than the average during the 1970s. We have identified some $10.2 billion, of which $5.3 billion is foreign and $4.9 billion is Canadian, plus $8.4 billion worth of unidentifiable capital which has left this country, all for a total of $18.6 billion.
I say to you, Sir, that the major part of this was caused by the Canadianization program, which was itself responsible for the outflow of $6.5 billion in the first six months of 1981. Unfortunately, that outflow is not slowing down. If you look at the outflow in the last quarter of 1981, Mr. Speaker, you will note that capital is flowing out at the same rate it did during the second quarter of 1981.
We have this risk-taking, productive capital leaving the country. It is being replaced by passive money seeking high interest rates in the form of bonds and bank deposits. It has been pointed out that some $5.6 billion in interest is flowing out of the country. It has also been pointed out that the failure of Canadianization is demonstrated by the fact that under the Canadianization program more money is now leaving the country to pay the interest than there was in the form of dividends paid out. This results in higher interest rates, pressure on the Canadian dollar, loss of jobs and a further loss of confidence in the economy.
That is clearly the central problem in Canada's economic woes, but it is clearly within the control and the responsibility of this government. It has not acted, but it must act. This outflow must stop. That is crucial if we are going to restore the kind of economic vitality that we need in this country. We need investment capital to stimulate production, to re-tool and to embark upon the various projects that are proposed but, indeed, at the present time are being stalled, postponed and delayed.
Other members in this House have made the following point: the outlook in this country is bleak. There is no hope. There is no promise. There is doom and gloom which is increasing day by day. There is a sense of despair in the country. Why is that? There are two reasons. First, the government does not appear to be addressing the problem. As a matter of fact, it is obvious the government is not addressing the problem; rather it is adding to the problem.
Second, we go back to the election campaign of 1980. One must go back because at that time there was the creation of false expectation. This government campaigned on a policy that was full of deceitful rhetoric. It promised cheap energy. It promosed lower interest rates. It promised a healthy economy. It promised a vibrant oil industry. The expectations were high. It was "elect us, and we will show you the way".
This goverment has not been able to show the way. This government's simple, slick solution has not worked. They have backfired. What do we have today, sir? We have the cancellation of Alsands, the cancellation of the Cold Lake Project, the
Borrowing Authority Act
cancellation of Judy Creek, the delay of the heavy oil upgrader in Saskatchewan and/or Alberta. We have the delay of the Alaska highway pipeline. We have a 40 per cent reduction in exploration and driling activities in western Canada, the result of which has thrown hundreds of thousands of Canadians out of work. Associated industries have gone bankrupt. The whole industry has collapsed. There has been an exodus of men, equipment, expertise and, indeed, capital.
The petrochemical industry is now another entity of the once vibrant petroleum industry that is now suffering. The latest edition of the "Alberta Report" cites "The Petrochemical Calamity; how Alberta's brightest industrial hope vanished overnight." And what are the chief reasons? There has been a slump in demand in global markets, primarily because of increased costs of petrochemical feedstock prices in Canada as a result of taxes and high interest rates. It has been a sobering situation for an industry which held such promise in Alberta. It was to be the star of the economy in 1980. It was to be the stimulus, the catalyst, that was going to diversify the economy of Alberta.
But the negative impacts of the National Energy Program in addition to the high interest rate policy and the very devasting provisions of the budget have thrown 13 out of 15 petrochemical projects into a state of limbo. I shall cite them for the record.
The Alberta Energy Company project of 1.1 billion pounds of benzene located at Bruderheim, worth $350 million, to be completed in 1984, is delayed while new partners are sought. Another Alberta Energy Company project also at Bruderheim, worth $300 million and to be completed in 1984, also delayed while new partners are sought.
AEC and Dupont Canada Inc. project for a low-density polyethylene plant at Redwater, worth $200 million; planned completion date 1984 and delayed six months.
The Alberta Gas Ethylene Co. project for 1.5 billion pounds of ethylene at Joffre, worth $590 million and due for completion in 1985, is delayed one year at least. The CIL and Trimac Ltd. Project worth $128 million is also delayed.
The Celanese Canada project worth $255 million, to be completed in 1982, also is delayed.
A Dow Chemical of Canada Ltd. project, a 180,000 tonne per year polyethylene plant at Fort Saskatchewan and worth $75 million, to be completed in 1984, is also delayed. Another Dow Chemical project worth $135 million, to be located also in Fort Saskatchewan and to be completed in 1984, also is delayed.
Gulf Canada Products Co. project, worth $250 million, is delayed in its early stages.
Enesco Chem Ltd. has two projects. One is worth $250 million and the other $240 million, both delayed, to be announced later.
Union Carbide Canada Ltd. has a $259 million project for ethylene glycol and it is further delayed.

Borrowing Authority Act
AEC, Esso Chem. and Hudson's Bay Oil and Gas, which had a $700 million project to be completed in 1986, is delayed indefinitely.
That is what is happening, Mr. Speaker. This government has killed the exploration industry. This government has killed the Canadian component of the industry. Now it is killing the petrochemical industry. The fact is that the National Energy Program has crippled and destroyed a once vibrant industry out there in Alberta. Mr. William Wilder, President of Hiram Walker Resources Ltd. has stated:
The NEP is just part of an approach to the economy of this country on the part of the federal government that is undermining the ability of every industry in Canada to meet the kinds of economic challenges it faces today-
Because federal policies have so eroded the real market attractions of investing in Canada, increasingly the only way we can attract money to keep our currency relatively strong is by paying historically high interest rates.
1 think that sums up the National Energy Program quite well. It has hurt the manufacturing industry, small business, the farmers and the workers.
As a matter of fact, I would like to read a letter that I received from one of my constituents, Mr. Henry C. Wilson, sales manager for Sun Life of Canada. He addressed his letter to the Prime Minister of Canada, a copy of which he forwarded to me. It reads:
As a Canadian of several generations I wish to ask you if you know what you are doing to this great country of ours? I write with respect to the re-election of your government in 1980, the introduction or nationalization of our country through programs such as NEP and thirdly with respect as a life underwriter, in the life insurance industry to the November 1981 budget and change in December 1981.
As in hockey, Sir, usually five players make a mistake before the goal keeper makes his. Canadians were first to make the mistake in re-electing you to govern our country again. You then had your chances and have made your mistakes many times since.
The NEP is a disguise I believe to socialize our country and it appears to be working better than you even planned I am sure. With the number of companies moving out of Canada or going broke, our wonderful Canadian Crown Companies will not even have to pay for some of the assets they will take over, simply pick up the keys. By the way, part of my tax dollar is in that Canadian Crown Company you have been playing with and I don't like it. As a result of NEP unemployment is higher than ever, as are corporate bankruptcy in our area of this country. This was before the budget of November 1981.
The Budget of November 1981 will kill any of the free enterprises or small businesses that were missed by the NEP.
It takes cash flow to purchase life insurance. My business today is 25 to 40 per cent of pre-November 1981. Do you know how many dollars this represents in Canada that are not flowing through the system to provide life insurance protection for families? Do you realize the dollars that life companies do not have today to finance homes, apartments, commercial buildings and finance industry-all these things that put people to work and lastly pay tax dollars to you to keep you flying around the world?
I write to suggest that you do two things very quickly to save our country.
(1)	Scrap the NEP.
(2)	Bring in a new budget that gives reward for work and provides incentive for people to put a dollar away for a rainy day-through life insurance or a deferred annuity as was pre-1981 income.
This gives us an idea of the depth of the feeling and the impact of the National Energy Program and of the budget upon average Canadians.
We know that the government's program for economic development is based upon resource megaprojects. Either
May 12, 1982
deliberately or through stupidity, economic leadership in the country has been such that economic infrastructure has been destroyed. Now we have a large number of potential megaprojects which were once on stream and are now down the tubes. I remind hon. members of the House that back in February, March and April of 1980 the oil industry was humming. At that time Alsands project was proceeding. It had the support of the Alberta government and the approval of the Alberta government and the approval of the Alberta Resources Conservation Board. As a matter of fact, it was working on site. The industry was humming, but it is now down the tubes as are so many others.
What about the alternatives? What will the government do now to pick up the slack? Will it make any fundamental changes to the National Energy program? The National Energy Program was referred to in the Edmonton Journal as "a real life nightmare". It went on to recite the deficiencies in it. The government must do something to refuel the engine for economic development upon which it has relied. If we are to alleviate the unemployment situation, there must be changes to the National Energy Program.
Mr. John D. Porter, management director of the Independent Petroleum Association of Canada, said recently that what was needed were some fundamental changes to the National Energy Program. He indicated the following:
(a)	Reduce the charges under the petroleum gas revenue tax.
(b)	Reduce the level of incremental oil revenue tax.
(c)	Reintroduce tax incentives so Canadians will invest in exploration and development in Canada.
(d)	Establish priority access to Canadian markets for Canadian crude oil production, thereby eliminating imports from foreign sources, thus reducing our balance of payments problem.
(e)	Open new long-term competitively priced natural gas export markets for Canadian producers at the earliest opportunity.
Those are some very logical and common sense recommendations which I suggest the government should consider seriously.
There are other options. We on the opposition side are looking for some answers. With the cancellation of the Alsands project, does it mean that efforts will now be redirected to revitalize the Cold Lake project or something similar to it, even though it would be on a smaller scale? 1 think this requires serious consideration.
Further, what will be the government's policy with respect to encouraging conventional oil drilling and exploration? Given the fact that supplies are dwindling, I believe serious consideration should be given to revitalizing that particular sector. What efforts will be made to commence in earnest a heavy oil upgrader? There are huge amounts of heavy oil shut in which we cannot now use because we do not have the facility to upgrade it to a level where it can be accepted by our conventional refiners. Now that Alsands has been cancelled, surely it is incumbent upon and behooves the government to reconsider and accelerate the establishment of a heavy oil upgrader in Alberta or Saskatchewan or both.
May 12, 1982

What plans does the government have with regard to establishing the kind of necessary initiatives toward enhanced recovery of heavy oil? There are huge deposits of heavy oil in Alberta and Saskatchewan. If we are to work toward achieving energy self-sufficiency, we certainly cannot wait until production is in place as far as the high Arctic, frontier lands and Hibernia are concerned. We have a long time to go before the regulations, the transportation system and all obstacles will be overcome. We must move toward revitalizing this very important sector. Since the announced cancellation of Alsands there has been nothing coming from the government in terms of what it proposes to do alternatively to take up the slack.
Finally, in order to end the uncertainty, the confusion and the devastation, the budget must clearly be withdrawn. I bring these recommendations to the attention of the House at this time in the interests of preserving and enhancing our leadership in technology in oil sands and heavy oil recovery. Also I bring them forth in the interests of ensuring adequate and secure supply, of aiding the restoration of our economic health and of looking at serious problems in regard to interest rates, the current account deficit and the outflow of capital to other countries. I bring forth these recommendations also in the interests of job creation and stimulated economic development and growth.
I believe these alternatives must be actively explored and that industry once again must be the major catalyst. The ground rules must be clearly spelled out. There must be stability and confidence. The government cannot move in and out and change rules in the middle of the night. There must be a clear set of rules, regulations and guidelines within which industry can function. We certainly cannot stand any more destruction and division as has occurred in the country over past years.
It is time to renew our economic and political partnership so that it will encourage production and growth, encourage the Canada first policy, reduce our dependence upon imports, and revitalize the private sector. We must attract new investment and ensure that investment dollars stay in the country. We must restore investor confidence and build upon our natural strengths. We have many natural strengths. 1 have talked mainly about the energy industry, but we also have agriculture, the oil industry and the mining industry. We have much potential in the country.
I should like to quote from a speech by Mr. Jim Gray, executive vice-president of Canadian Hunter Exploration in Calgary. He said:
This country is languishing in a state of economic gloom and political rancour.
Entrepreneurship and free enterprise are out of fashion in the decision-making regions and cities of Canada. The centralization of political decision-making in government offices, especially in Ottawa, is apparently the new process for building one Canada.
Quite obviously it is a process that, because it is designed to centralize power in Ottawa, is in direct conflict with regional decision-making. An inevitable result is serious tension.
Canada today is a game played by and for bureaucrats and government theorists. We were once a great nation of producers and entrepreneurs. The hands that once drove industry and created jobs now spend weeks out of every year in the stroking of politicians.
Borrowing Authority Act
The builders that once spent all their time driving production on the drilling rigs, at the mine site or on the factory floor now sit, cap in hand and hour by hour, in the outer offices of the Ottawa bureaucrats. They are waiting for their decisions as to the tax regime and regulations under which the entrepreneur will operate and strive to create jobs and production and make a profit.
This is a very, very sad litany of what has happened. The enterprise spirit in the country has been destroyed. Unless the government fundamentally changes its direction, that spirit will be destroyed to the extent that it will be very difficult for any government, even a Conservative government, to recover and redirect.
